Guide 02 / 10

Reading an appliance power label accurately

Find the relevant input rating and see why a label is not the same as a real-world energy measurement.

Vijeron · Updated 9 October 2026

Look for electrical input

For an electricity estimate, find input power in W or kW on the rating plate, manual, or specification sheet. Do not substitute an output figure such as brightness or cooling capacity. Those describe what a device delivers, not necessarily what it draws from an outlet.

Account for operating modes

A device may draw different power when active, on standby, or apparently off but still plugged in. Heating and cooling appliances can cycle automatically. A maximum rating can help identify an upper operating limit but may exaggerate energy use if treated as the draw at every minute.

Measure when it matters

A suitable plug-in energy meter can record kWh over several days for a device you want to compare. Follow the meter's safety instructions and stay within its capacity. Compare readings under similar usage patterns.

A worked example

Example: an 800 W label does not establish that the appliance draws 800 W all day. Use actual run time or measured kWh.

Avoid this mistake

Common error: treating an output capacity figure as electrical input watts.
